Antibodies are produced by B cells (also called B lymphocytes), a type of white blood cell and one of the two main types of lymphocytes [d1][d7]. When activated by an antigen, B cells divide and differentiate into plasma cells, which are the primary antibody-secreting effector cells [d3][d6]. According to NCBI, antibodies are "synthesized exclusively by B cells," and plasma cells can secrete antibodies at the astonishing rate of about 2,000 molecules per second, with some plasma cells surviving in the bone marrow for months or years [d2]. B lymphocytes initially develop in the bone marrow and, once mature, travel to lymphatic organs such as the spleen and lymph nodes, where they can be activated to produce antibodies that circulate in the bloodstream and lymph system [d3][d6][d9].
